claims.text: The starting material is a near-equimolar mixture of noble-metal precursors intended to form an HEA.
Rapid post-synthesis quenching limits atomic diffusion relative to slow cooling.
Suppressing atomic diffusion during formation can favor a homogeneous solid-solution HEA rather than a segregated structure.
Rapid quenching produces more homogeneous noble-metal HEA nanoparticles than slow cooling.
Slow cooling permits sufficient atomic diffusion to cause partial phase segregation.
A well-mixed HEA structure can create highly dispersed or isolated noble-metal active sites.
Isolated Pt and Pd sites in a PtPdCoCuNi HEA exhibit altered electronic properties and stronger interaction with nitrobenzene.
The electronic properties arising from alloying and isolated active sites can enhance nitrobenzene hydrogenation activity.
Phase segregation diminishes the synergistic electronic effects responsible for enhanced catalytic activity.
Homogeneous platinum-group-metal HEA nanocrystals can outperform phase-separated counterparts in catalytic activity and durability.
Rapidly quenched samples will have a higher catalytic turnover frequency than otherwise identical slow-cooled samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will have higher product selectivity than otherwise identical slow-cooled samples.
The proposed cooling-rate effect should hold for noble-metal precursor mixtures synthesized at 100–300°C under reducing atmospheres and fixed reaction times.
Cooling rate can be isolated experimentally by holding precursor composition, synthesis conditions, and reaction time constant.
XRD and TEM can be used to compare structural homogeneity and phase segregation between the samples.
The magnitude of the catalytic difference may depend on precursor composition and incompletely characterized kinetic effects.
Failure of the rapidly quenched samples to show statistically significant improvements in both structural homogeneity and catalytic performance would falsify the hypothesis.
